quests.question: I have three ___ in my bag.
quests.hint: Nouns ending in -x, -ch, -sh, -ss add -es in the plural.
quests.explanation: Nouns ending in -x, -ch, -sh, -ss add '-es': box → boxes, watch → watches, dish → dishes, class → classes. Regular nouns just add '-s': book → books.

quests.question: There are two ___ in the garden.
quests.hint: 'Child' has an irregular plural - it does not add -s.
quests.explanation: 'Child' has the irregular plural 'children'. Other irregular plurals: man → men, woman → women, tooth → teeth, foot → feet, mouse → mice. These must be memorised.

quests.question: She has five ___.
quests.hint: Most nouns ending in a vowel + -o just add -s.
quests.explanation: Most nouns ending in -o add '-s': photo → photos, video → videos, piano → pianos. Some add '-es': potato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes. 'Photos' is correct.

quests.question: Mount Everest is ___ than any other mountain.
quests.hint: Short adjectives (one syllable) add -er for comparatives.
quests.explanation: Short adjectives add '-er' for comparatives: tall → taller, fast → faster, big → bigger. Always use 'than' after the comparative: taller than. Long adjectives use 'more': more interesting.

quests.question: This exam is ___ than I expected.
quests.hint: Long adjectives use 'more' for comparatives.
quests.explanation: Adjectives with three or more syllables use 'more' for comparatives: more difficult, more interesting, more expensive. Never 'difficulter' - that's a common error.

quests.question: Today is ___ day of the year.
quests.hint: Superlatives need 'the' before them.
quests.explanation: Superlatives say something is at the top level. One-syllable adjectives: add '-est' with 'the': the hottest, the tallest, the biggest. Note the doubled consonant in 'hottest' (consonant-vowel-consonant rule).

quests.question: My sister ___ speak four languages.
quests.hint: Modal verbs never add -s for third person.
quests.explanation: 'Can' is a modal verb and never changes form. We never say 'cans' or 'she cans'. It is always 'can' for all subjects: I can, she can, they can. Modal verbs are always followed by the base verb.

quests.question: ___ you swim?
quests.hint: Use the modal verb to ask about ability.
quests.explanation: Use 'Can' to ask about ability: Can you swim? Don't say 'Do you can swim?' Modal verbs form questions by inverting with the subject: Can you...? Will she...? Should we...?

quests.question: He ___ lift heavy boxes at all.
quests.hint: 'At all' signals a negative meaning - use 'can't'.
quests.explanation: 'Can't' = cannot. 'He can't lift heavy boxes at all' means he is completely unable to. 'At all' makes a negative stronger: I can't sleep at all. I don't understand it at all.

quests.question: She is wearing ___ dress.
quests.hint: In English, the article comes first, then adjectives, then the noun.
quests.explanation: English word order for noun phrases: article (a/the) + adjectives + noun. So: a beautiful red dress. The adjective comes between the article and the noun. Never 'a dress beautiful'.

quests.question: The ___ gave an interesting lecture.
quests.hint: Adjectives come directly before the noun.
quests.explanation: Adjectives come before nouns: the old teacher, not 'the teacher old'. The article (the) comes before the adjective: the + old + teacher. This is the basic English noun phrase order.

quests.question: It was ___ night.
quests.hint: Multiple adjectives follow a general order: quality → temperature → general.
quests.explanation: English has a standard adjective order: cold (temperature) + dark (general description/light) + stormy (condition/weather): a cold, dark, stormy night. The general order is: opinion → size → age → temperature → colour → origin.

quests.question: ___ does she live?
quests.hint: This question asks about a place.
quests.explanation: Question words: Where = place, When = time, What = thing or action, Who = person, Why = reason, How = manner. 'Where does she live?' asks about her location.

quests.question: ___ is your favourite colour?
quests.hint: This asks about a thing - which word is used for things?
quests.explanation: 'What' asks about things, objects, ideas, or general information: What is your name? What colour do you like? What time is it? Use 'Who' for people: Who is that?

quests.question: ___ did they arrive so late?
quests.hint: This question expects an answer explaining a reason.
quests.explanation: 'Why' asks for a reason or cause: Why are you late? → Because I missed the bus. Don't confuse 'Why' (reason) with 'When' (time) or 'Where' (place).

quests.question: She ___ eats breakfast.
quests.hint: The sentence means she eats breakfast 100% of the time.
quests.explanation: Frequency adverbs: always (100%), usually (80%), often (60%), sometimes (40%), rarely (20%), never (0%). They go before the main verb but after 'be': She always eats breakfast. He is always late.

quests.question: He is ___ late for work.
quests.hint: With the verb 'be', frequency adverbs come after it.
quests.explanation: With 'be', frequency adverbs come AFTER the verb: He is always late. He is never early. With other verbs, they come BEFORE: He always arrives late. He never misses a meeting.

quests.question: I ___ miss the bus - I'm always on time.
quests.hint: If you're always on time, how often do you miss the bus?
quests.explanation: If you are 'always on time', you 'never' miss the bus. Never = 0% of the time. Always = 100%. The two parts of the sentence must be logically consistent.

quests.question: Look! The children ___ in the rain.
quests.hint: 'Look!' signals something happening right now.
quests.explanation: Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) describes actions happening right now. Signal words: look!, now, at the moment, currently. 'The children are playing' = they are doing it right now.

quests.question: She ___ a book at the moment.
quests.hint: 'At the moment' tells you the action is happening now.
quests.explanation: 'At the moment' signals present continuous. Form: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. 'She is reading a book at the moment.' Not just 'reading' - you need the auxiliary 'is'.

quests.question: I ___ to music while I cook.
quests.hint: Present continuous with 'I' uses 'am'.
quests.explanation: For present continuous: I + am, He/She/It + is, You/We/They + are. 'I am listening to music while I cook.' Never 'I is' or 'I are'.

quests.question: They ___ visit their grandparents next weekend.
quests.hint: 'Going to' needs a 'be' verb before it.
quests.explanation: 'Going to' requires the verb 'be': I am going to, He is going to, They are going to. Use 'going to' for decided plans or intentions: They are going to visit their grandparents.

quests.question: She ___ study medicine at university.
quests.hint: She has already decided - use 'be going to' for pre-made plans.
quests.explanation: Use 'be going to' when a decision was made before the moment of speaking: She is going to study medicine. Use 'will' for spontaneous decisions: Oh, I'll help you! (decided right now).

quests.question: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
quests.hint: We can see clouds - visible evidence points to 'going to'.
quests.explanation: Use 'going to' when there is visible evidence for a prediction: Look at the clouds - it is going to rain! Use 'will' for general predictions with no visible evidence: I think it will rain tomorrow.

quests.question: I was tired, ___ I went to bed early.
quests.hint: The second clause shows a result of the first.
quests.explanation: 'So' connects a cause and its result: I was tired, so I went to bed early. 'But' shows contrast. 'Because' explains a reason. 'Or' offers an alternative. 'So' = result.

quests.question: She loves dancing, ___ she hates singing.
quests.hint: These two ideas are opposite - which word shows contrast?
quests.explanation: 'But' shows contrast between two ideas: She loves dancing, but she hates singing. Use 'and' to add similar ideas, 'because' for reasons, and 'so' for results.

quests.question: He passed the exam ___ he studied hard.
quests.hint: The second clause explains why he passed.
quests.explanation: 'Because' introduces a reason: He passed because he studied hard. Don't confuse 'because' (conjunction + clause) with 'because of' (preposition + noun phrase: because of his hard work).

quests.question: She ___ like spicy food.
quests.hint: Third person singular uses 'doesn't' in negative sentences.
quests.explanation: In simple present negative, use 'doesn't' for he/she/it and 'don't' for I/you/we/they. The main verb stays in base form: She doesn't like (not 'She doesn't likes').

quests.question: They ___ at home right now - they're at work.
quests.hint: 'Be' doesn't use 'don't'/'doesn't' - it takes 'not' directly.
quests.explanation: To make 'be' negative, add 'not' after it: They are not = They aren't. Never 'They don't be'. 'Don't'/'doesn't' is only used with action verbs (like, want, know), not with 'be'.

quests.question: I ___ finished my homework yet.
quests.hint: 'Yet' is a signal word for present perfect.
quests.explanation: 'Yet' is used with present perfect. Negative present perfect: have/has + not = haven't/hasn't. 'I haven't finished my homework yet.' 'Yet' goes at the end of the sentence.
